issues.legal_issue: A will is not duly proved when the attesting witness examined does not establish attestation by both witnesses and another available attesting witness is not examined.
material_facts: The will was required to be attested by two witnesses.
Only one attesting witness was examined; he did not establish that the other witness attested the will in his presence and said he had not seen the other witness at execution.
The other attesting witness was alive, and no attempt to examine him or impediment to doing so was shown.
issues.conclusion: The evidence of the one attesting witness did not prove due execution of the will; the other available attesting witness had to be called, and the will was not proved.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will must be attested by two or more witnesses in the specified manner. Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, permits proof through one attesting witness, but that witness must establish due execution, including attestation by both witnesses. If that witness does not, another available attesting witness must be called to supplement the evidence. The Court relied on and approved Vishnu Ramkrishna v. Nathu Vithal (AIR 1949 Bom. 266).

rule.if: will_proof_proceeding and only_one_attesting_witness_examined and witness_did_not_prove_both_attestations and other_attesting_witness_available and other_attesting_witness_not_examined

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A party sought to establish a will in court.
predicates.only_one_attesting_witness_examined: The party seeking to prove the will examined only one of its attesting witnesses.
predicates.witness_did_not_prove_both_attestations: The examined witness did not establish that both witnesses attested the will in the required manner.
predicates.other_attesting_witness_available: The other attesting witness was alive and capable of being called to give evidence.
predicates.other_attesting_witness_not_examined: The party seeking to prove the will did not examine the other available attesting witness.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to prove a will, examines one attesting witness who does not establish both attestations, and leaves another available attesting witness unexamined, the will is not proved as duly executed.

issues.legal_issue: The fallback of proving execution through other evidence does not excuse failure to examine another available attesting witness when the witness called does not prove due execution.
material_facts: The sole attesting witness examined did not prove that the other attesting witness had attested the will.
The other attesting witness was available but was not called.
The party seeking to prove the will relied on testimony from other witnesses, including the scribe.
issues.conclusion: Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act did not permit the party to substitute other evidence for the unexamined, available attesting witness in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, is a safeguard that permits other evidence when an attesting witness who has been called denies or does not recollect execution and the party is otherwise unable to prove it through the attesting witnesses. It does not relieve a party of the requirements of Section 68 when another attesting witness is available but has not been called. The Court approved the approach in Vishnu Ramkrishna v. Nathu Vithal (AIR 1949 Bom. 266) and held the view in Mt. Manki Kaur v. Hansraj Singh (AIR 1938 Pat. 301) on Section 71 to be incorrect.

rule.if: will_proof_proceeding and attesting_witness_called and witness_failed_to_prove_due_execution and other_attesting_witness_available and other_attesting_witness_not_examined

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A party sought to establish a will in court.
predicates.attesting_witness_called: The party seeking to prove the will called an attesting witness to testify.
predicates.witness_failed_to_prove_due_execution: The witness called did not establish execution of the will with the required attestations.
predicates.other_attesting_witness_available: Another attesting witness was alive and capable of being called to give evidence.
predicates.other_attesting_witness_not_examined: The party seeking to prove the will did not examine the other available attesting witness.

issues.definition: When a party seeking to prove a will calls an attesting witness who fails to prove due execution but leaves another available attesting witness unexamined, other evidence cannot substitute for that witness.

issues.legal_issue: A person who signs a will only as its scribe, without an intention to attest it, cannot be treated as an attesting witness.
material_facts: The person who prepared the will testified that he signed it as its scribe.
The evidence contained no indication that he intended his signature to attest the will.
The court below treated the scribe as an attesting witness.
issues.conclusion: The scribe could not be treated as an attesting witness on the evidence in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, requires attestation by witnesses who sign the will in the prescribed manner. The evidence must show that the signer acted with an intention to attest; signing in the capacity of scribe alone does not establish that intention. The Court confined its finding to the evidence in this case and did not decide whether a scribe could qualify as an attesting witness in other circumstances.

rule.if: will_proof_proceeding and signer_prepared_will and signer_signed_only_as_scribe and no_intention_to_attest_shown

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A party sought to establish a will in court.
predicates.signer_prepared_will: The person whose signature was relied on prepared or wrote the will.
predicates.signer_signed_only_as_scribe: The person testified that the signature was made in the capacity of scribe.
predicates.no_intention_to_attest_shown: The evidence did not show that the person intended the signature to attest the will.

issues.definition: When a person prepared a will, signed it only as scribe, and no intention to attest is shown, that person is not established as an attesting witness.

issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court cannot reverse a first appellate court's fact finding, based on proper objective appreciation of the evidence, without identifying a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The first appellate court assessed the evidence and found that due execution of the will had not been proved.
The second appellate court reversed that finding and restored the trial court's decree.
The second appellate court did not identify a substantial question of law for consideration.
issues.conclusion: The second appellate court's reversal was erroneous and could not stand; the first appellate court's judgment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: In a second appeal, reversal of a first appellate court's fact finding that rests on proper and objective appreciation of the evidence requires a substantial question of law for consideration. The Court found that none had been indicated in this case.

rule.if: second_appeal_proceeding and first_appellate_finding_based_on_proper_evidence_assessment and second_appellate_court_reversed_finding and no_substantial_question_of_law_identified

predicates.second_appeal_proceeding: The matter was before a court hearing a second appeal.
predicates.first_appellate_finding_based_on_proper_: The first appellate court's finding rested on proper and objective assessment of the evidence.
predicates.second_appellate_court_reversed_finding: The second appellate court reversed the first appellate court's finding.
predicates.no_substantial_question_of_law_identifie: The second appellate court did not identify a substantial question of law for consideration.

issues.definition: When a second appellate court reverses a first appellate court's finding based on proper evidence assessment without identifying a substantial question of law, that reversal is not sustainable.
